draft.body:
Dear Professor Oki,

Your Noh audience research plan combines questionnaires and physiological responses with a real/VR-space comparison (https://educ.titech.ac.jp/ee/eng/news/2023_04/064193.html). That makes the transfer between simulated and physical spatial experience especially relevant.

I’m developing Proxy Society, an architecture research project on AI agents and robots acting for absent people under limited, revocable mandates. In a proposed library arrival study, VR would vary whether a staffed help point is visible from an AI proxy’s waiting position; a full-scale mock-up would test revocation and human handoff. Ordinary booking, fixed automation and human assistance would provide controls, while personal attendance remains possible.

Would this comparison fit your lab’s architectural evaluation work, and what evidence should a research plan establish before the interview? I would prepare the CV, motivation and plan required by your contact page.

Best regards,
Kris Haamer

Your published bibliography lists a 2025 study of urban spatial images in photo-based Tokyo directions (https://shiozaki.main.jp/). It suggests a useful question about how a depicted route differs from the space someone encounters.

I’m developing Proxy Society, an architecture research project on AI agents and robots acting for absent people under limited, revocable mandates. Comparing shared and separate waiting edges would test whether mandate expiry and a staffed handoff can be understood without excluding the visitor.

Could you advise whether authority and revocation should be represented within Common Ground, and which failure scenario would best test that representation? I would also value guidance on a future doctoral route and supervision continuity beyond the term noted in the current guide.

Dear Professor Matsuda,

Your laboratory connects observation of users’ needs with universal design, including spaces for outings and rest for people with visual impairment: https://arch.t.u-tokyo.ac.jp/en/laboratory/matsuda-lab/. This suggests that the layout should be tested before treating robotic assistance as an improvement.

I’m developing Architecture of Delegated Presence as a PhD proposal. At a library entrance, an AI/robot could collect a reserved book for an absent person with a limited mandate that expires or can be revoked. I would compare a shared counter with a separate handoff bay, keeping the tactile route, rest seat and staffed service accessible to people arriving themselves.

Could you advise which user needs and observation measures would reveal whether delegation changes waiting, orientation or staff assistance? I would value your critique of an accessible test protocol and guidance on an appropriate future research or doctoral route.

Best regards,
Kris Haamer
